html:
A great French encyclopedia published from 1751 to 1772 under Denis Diderot and, for the early volumes, the mathematician Jean le Rond d'Alembert. It aimed to gather all human knowledge and became the flagship of the Enlightenment.

It began as a plan to translate an English work, the Cyclopaedia of Ephraim Chambers, and grew into something much bigger: 17 volumes of text and 11 of plates. The plates showed crafts and trades in detail, from printing to glassmaking, and treated working skills as knowledge worth recording.

Over 130 writers took part, including Voltaire, Rousseau and Montesquieu. Its articles praised reason, science and tolerance, and often slipped criticism of the church and the crown into odd corners, such as cross references. The authorities banned it in 1759, and Diderot carried on almost alone, partly in secret.

Its ideas spread among the educated across Europe, and Catherine the Great offered to have it printed in Russia. Many saw it as preparing the ground for the French Revolution.
